propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of IRCC Officer's January 22, 2020 decision refusing permanent residence due to criminal inadmissibility.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Mr. Carl Anderson Adams, seeks judicial review of a January 22, 2020 decision [Decision] of an Officer of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada [IRCC] that refused his application for permanent residence as a member of the Spouse or Common-law Partner in Canada class, on the basis of inadmissibility for criminality under paragraph 36(2)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant seeks judicial review of a January 22, 2020 IRCC decision refusing permanent residence due to criminal inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Issue is whether the applicant was denied procedural fairness regarding an extension request for rehabilitation application.
propositions.quote: The issue before the Court is whether the Applicant was denied procedural fairness. The Applicant asserts that a request for an extension of time to file a rehabilitation application was properly made, but was not considered by the Officer who made the Decision.

propositions.text: Applicant asserts he properly made a request for extension of time to file rehabilitation application which was not considered.
propositions.quote: The Applicant asserts that a request for an extension of time to file a rehabilitation application was properly made, but was not considered by the Officer who made the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is procedural fairness; the applicant argues his extension request was properly made but not considered.

propositions.text: Finds no evidence that extension request was pending or any procedural fairness breach; application dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I find that the evidence does not support a finding that a request for an extension of time was pending before the Officer when the Decision was made or that there has been any breach of procedural fairness. As such, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of a pending extension request or procedural fairness breach and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Applicant, a Barbados citizen, entered Canada March 3, 2016 as visitor, overstayed after May 30, 2017 permit expiry.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, a citizen of Barbados, entered Canada as a visitor on March 3, 2016. He did not extend his temporary resident permit, which expired on May 30, 2017, and remained in Canada without authorization.

propositions.text: Applicant married sponsor February 12, 2017 and applied for permanent residence July 18, 2017 under Spouse in Canada class.
propositions.quote: The Applicant married his sponsor on February 12, 2017 and applied for permanent residence in Canada under the Spouse in Canada class on July 18, 2017.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant entered Canada as visitor in 2016, overstayed, married sponsor in 2017, and applied for permanent residence.

propositions.text: On December 7, 2019, applicant received procedural fairness letter about inadmissibility due to prior Barbados convictions.
propositions.quote: On December 7, 2019, the Applicant received a procedural fairness letter [PFL] informing him of his potential inadmissibility due to prior convictions in Barbados from 2001 and 2004.

propositions.text: Officer equated convictions to indictable offences under Criminal Code and said deemed rehabilitation not possible but individual rehabilitation might be.
propositions.quote: The Officer equated these convictions to indictable offences under the Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46 and indicated that the Applicant would not be eligible for deemed rehabilitation, although individual rehabilitation might be possible.

propositions.text: PFL gave 30 days to submit rehabilitation application and warned refusal if none submitted or further submissions made.
propositions.quote: The PFL gave the Applicant 30 days to submit a rehabilitation application. The PFL indicated that if the Applicant did not apply for rehabilitation or make any further submissions, then a decision regarding the Applicant’s compliance with the IRPA would be made based on the information on file, and might result in a refusal of the permanent residence application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant received a procedural fairness letter on December 7, 2019 about inadmissibility and 30-day rehabilitation application deadline.

propositions.text: On January 6, 2020, applicant emailed IRCC asking for leniency and reconsideration citing time lapse and family circumstances.
propositions.quote: On January 6, 2020, the day of the deadline under the PFL, the Applicant sent an email to the IRCC asking for leniency and reconsideration of his application in view of the lapse of time since his offences and his more recent circumstances and behaviour, including his family situation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant emailed IRCC on January 6, 2020 asking for leniency and reconsideration due to time lapse and family circumstances.

propositions.text: On January 22, 2020, Officer issued decision considering January 6 email but found no rehabilitation application filed, so applicant inadmissible.
propositions.quote: On January 22, 2020, the Officer issued the Decision. The Officer considered the January 6, 2020 email, but found that as no rehabilitation application had been filed, the Applicant was inadmissible.

propositions.text: Officer also considered but did not grant humanitarian and compassionate exemption, though not specifically requested.
propositions.quote: Although not specifically requested, the Officer also went on to consider that there were insufficient grounds to justify granting an exemption for Humanitarian and Compassionate reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer issued decision on January 22, 2020, considered January 6 email but found no rehabilitation application and denied humanitarian exemption.

propositions.text: Applicant submits affidavit claiming he emailed extension request on January 2, 2020, and failure to consider it breaches procedural fairness.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has submitted an affidavit in this judicial review proceeding, contending that he sent a letter by email attachment to IRCC on January 2, 2020, requesting an extension of time to obtain the documents required for a rehabilitation application. The Applicant argues that the failure of the Officer to acknowledge and consider his request for an extension of time constitutes a breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submits affidavit claiming he emailed extension request on January 2, 2020 and alleges procedural fairness breach for non-consideration.

propositions.text: Respondent disputes receiving extension letter and submits affidavit stating no email found in IRCC inbox after search.
propositions.quote: The Respondent disputes that any extension letter was received by the IRCC and has submitted an affidavit from an Operations Manager of the IRCC [Thyriar Affidavit] stating that a search of the general inbox was made, but that no email was received.

propositions.text: Thyriar Affidavit relies on information from Officer who made decision and supervisor of Officer’s unit.
propositions.quote: The Thyriar Affidavit relies on information and belief from the Officer who rendered the Decision and from the supervisor of the Officer’s unit.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent disputes receiving extension letter and submits affidavit stating no email found in IRCC inbox, relying on Officer and supervisor information.

propositions.text: Sole issue is whether applicant was denied procedural fairness by ignoring extension request before Officer.
propositions.quote: The sole issue raised by this judicial review is whether the Applicant has been denied procedural fairness. To address this issue, the Court must determine whether there was a request for an extension of time to submit a rehabilitation application before the Officer that went unanswered.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the sole issue is whether the applicant was denied procedural fairness by ignoring an extension request before the Officer.

propositions.text: Standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness, focusing on fairness and justice of procedure followed.
propositions.quote: The standard of review for questions of procedural fairness is best reflected by the correctness standard, although they are not strictly speaking subject to a standard of review analysis. Instead, such questions are to be reviewed from the perspective of whether the procedure followed by the decision-maker was fair and just: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (AG), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54; Canadian Association of Refugee Lawyers v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2020 FCA 196 at para 35; Sangha v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 95 at para 13.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness, assessing fairness and justice of procedure.

propositions.text: Reasonable, timely extension requests pending before Officer should be considered before decision is made.
propositions.quote: The parties agree that where a reasonable and timely request for an extension of time has been made and is pending before an Officer, the request should be considered before a decision is made (Venkata v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 423 at paras 75-76; Hussain v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1199 at paras 6-11; Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1999] SCR 817).

paragraphs.summary: The court states reasonable, timely extension requests pending before Officer must be considered before decision.

propositions.text: Applicant contends affidavit evidence suffices to presume extension request was received and pending.
propositions.quote: The Applicant contends that his affidavit evidence is sufficient to establish that a request for an extension of time was sent to the IRCC. As such, it should be presumed that the request was received and pending.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant contends his affidavit suffices to presume the extension request was received and pending.

propositions.text: Applicant cites cases presuming email sent to address on file is received unless rebutted by evidence.
propositions.quote: The Applicant refers to Karimi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1163 at paragraphs 10-11 and Ghaloghlyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 1252 at paragraphs 8-10, which dealt with the issue of the burden placed on the respondent to establish email correspondence was sent from an officer to an applicant where there was an assertion from the applicant that the communication was not received. In those cases, once it was shown that the email correspondence was sent to the address on file and was “on its way”, it was presumed to be received, unless rebutted and established otherwise by the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant cites cases presuming emails sent to address on file are received unless rebutted by evidence.

propositions.text: Respondent asserts applicant has not met burden to prove extension request was before Officer.
propositions.quote: The Respondent asserts that the Applicant has not met his burden to establish that an extension request was before the Officer.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent asserts the applicant has not met burden to prove extension request was before the Officer.

propositions.text: Respondent relies on Asoyan recognizing email less reliable than fax; sender must exhaust reasonable mechanisms to ensure receipt.
propositions.quote: It relies on Asoyan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 206 [Asoyan]. In Asoyan, at paragraph 24, it was recognized that email communication does not lend to the same reliability of receipt as facsimile. As such, it was proposed that the sender’s obligations should be broader and should include exhausting reasonable mechanisms on email programs to ensure email transmissions are received (see also Patel v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 900 at para 34).

paragraphs.summary: The respondent relies on Asoyan that email is less reliable than fax and sender must exhaust reasonable means to ensure receipt.

propositions.text: Asoyan recognized subsequent correspondence may indicate if email was received; sender may need to follow up if not.
propositions.quote: In Asoyan, at paragraphs 18-19, it was recognized that subsequent correspondence between the parties in question may be informative as to whether email correspondence has been received. Where there is an indication that it has not, it may require follow-up by the sender.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent notes Asoyan recognized subsequent correspondence may show if email was received and sender may need to follow up.

propositions.text: Correspondence from applicant to respondent was not included in Certified Tribunal Record before Officer.
propositions.quote: The correspondence in question here is from the Applicant to the Respondent. It was not included by the Respondent in the Certified Tribunal Record [CTR] as being a document that was before the Officer who rendered the Decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the correspondence from applicant to respondent was not included in the Certified Tribunal Record before the Officer.

propositions.text: Documents not in Certified Tribunal Record presumed not before Officer unless applicant proves otherwise; burden on applicant.
propositions.quote: It is well established that where a document does not appear in the CTR, the Court will presume that the document was not before the immigration officer, unless there is evidence from the applicant establishing the contrary. A bare assertion is not enough. The burden lies with the applicant to demonstrate that the document was before the decision-maker (Adewale v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 1190 at para 11; El Dor c Canada (Citoyenneté et de l’Immigration), 2015 FC 1406 at para 32; Togtokh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 581 at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court states documents not in Certified Tribunal Record are presumed not before Officer unless applicant proves otherwise; burden is on applicant.

propositions.text: Applicant submitted affidavit stating extension request letter was emailed January 2, 2020 with printout from spouse’s Gmail showing message to IRCC.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Applicant has submitted an affidavit, which states that an extension request letter was sent as an attachment by email on January 2, 2020. The affidavit attaches as an exhibit a printout from the Applicant’s spouse’s Gmail account, showing an unlabelled message from January 2, 2020 at 08:42 to the IRCC email address.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant submitted affidavit stating extension request emailed January 2, 2020 with Gmail printout showing message to IRCC.

propositions.text: No identifiers on the January 2, 2020 email indicate its subject or connection to an active IRCC file, and the attachment is unlabeled.
propositions.quote: there are no identifiers on the email to indicate what the message is about or that it pertains to an active IRCC file, and there is no content to the email. The printout shows only that the message has a document attachment, but the document is not labelled with any identifier.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the January 2, 2020 email lacks identifiers and its attachment is unlabeled.

propositions.text: Neither the email printout nor the attached document indicate that the letter is 'Document (5)'.
propositions.quote: neither the email printout nor the document itself indicate that this letter is “Document (5)”

propositions.text: The Respondent argues the letter is not 'Document (5)'.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent, that neither the email printout nor the document itself indicate that this letter is “Document (5)”

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with the Respondent that the letter is not identified as 'Document (5)'.

propositions.text: No acknowledgement or read receipt accompanies the January 2, 2020 email, and it is unclear if the printout is from a sent box or if there was a bounce-back.
propositions.quote: The January 2, 2020 email is not accompanied by an acknowledgement of receipt or confirmation of read receipt and there is no printout from the email inbox to show that there was no bounce-back to the message. It is unclear from the printout whether it is a printout of the message from an email sent box.

propositions.text: The affidavit does not address whether the email was properly sent or received.
propositions.quote: The affidavit does not speak to this issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no receipt confirmation for the January 2 email and the affidavit does not clarify its status.

propositions.text: Other evidence suggests the January 2, 2020 message was not properly received or pursued by the Applicant.
propositions.quote: Other evidence from the record suggests that any January 2, 2020 message was not properly received and was not pursued in follow-up by the Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence suggests the January 2 message was not received or followed up by the Applicant.

propositions.text: The Applicant acknowledges no response was received to the January 2 email but attaches a January 7 confirmation for a January 6 email.
propositions.quote: the Applicant acknowledges that he did not receive any response to the proposed January 2, 2020 email. In contrast, he attaches a confirmation of receipt received from the IRCC five days later, on January 7, 2020, to the separate email submission made on January 6, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant admits no response to the January 2 email but shows a January 7 receipt for a January 6 email.

propositions.text: Lack of identifiers and no acknowledgement of the January 2 email casts doubt it was recognized or received by IRCC.
propositions.quote: The lack of identifiers on the January 2, 2020 email and the fact that it was not acknowledged, when the separate email response sent four days later was acknowledged the very next day, casts serious doubt that any earlier message was recognized and properly received by the IRCC.

paragraphs.summary: The court doubts the January 2 email was recognized or received by IRCC due to lack of identifiers and no acknowledgement.

propositions.text: The January 6 email does not suggest the Applicant was pursuing an extension or referencing the January 2 email.
propositions.quote: The Applicant’s January 6, 2020 email informally responded to the PFL without any mention of the January 2, 2020 correspondence, a requested extension, or any continuing efforts by the Applicant to obtain documents from Barbados for the purpose of compiling a rehabilitation application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the January 6 email does not indicate pursuit of an extension or mention the January 2 email.

propositions.text: No evidence shows the Applicant followed up on any extension request before or after the Decision, which would be expected.
propositions.quote: There is no evidence that the Applicant did any follow-up with the IRCC as to the status of any pending extension request either before or after the Decision. Some follow-up from the Applicant would have been expected in these circumstances, particularly where the extension was of such importance and no response to the request was received.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of Applicant follow-up on extension requests, which would be expected.

propositions.text: The Respondent asserts it did not receive the January 2 email and submits the Thyriar Affidavit.
propositions.quote: The Respondent asserts that it did not receive the Applicant’s January 2, 2020 email. It submits the Thyriar Affidavit in support of this assertion.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the Thyriar Affidavit should be struck or given little weight as hearsay.
propositions.quote: The Applicant argues that the Thyriar Affidavit should be struck, or in the alternative afforded little weight, as it is largely based on hearsay evidence.

propositions.text: The Thyriar Affidavit has limited weight due to inconsistencies and hearsay but this does not affect the outcome.
propositions.quote: While I agree that the Thyriar Affidavit can only be given limited weight in view of inconsistencies and its reliance on information and belief, in my view this is of no moment.

propositions.text: Applicant has not met burden to show extension request was before Officer at Decision time; no procedural fairness breach found.
propositions.quote: The Applicant has not met his burden of establishing that an extension request was before the Officer at the time of the Decision. As such, there is no basis for finding a breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent says it did not receive the January 2 email; the Applicant challenges the affidavit; the court gives affidavit limited weight but finds no procedural fairness breach.

propositions.text: No argument that the Decision was unreasonable; findings suffice to dismiss the application.
propositions.quote: As there was no argument raised that the Decision was otherwise unreasonable, these findings are sufficient to dismiss the application.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application as no unreasonableness argument was raised and findings suffice.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed.
propositions.quote: The application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application.

propositions.text: No question for certification was proposed or arises; judicial review application dismissed.
propositions.quote: No question for certification was proposed by the parties and none arises in this case. JUDGMENT IN IMM-886-20 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application and certifies no question of general importance.
